title: Go-To-Market Brief: Launching a New Product
prompt: Write a go-to-market brief for a product launch. The company is an established project-management SaaS whose new product is an AI-powered meeting-notes and action-item assistant that integrates with its existing tool. It will launch in one quarter. Produce a concise, leadership-ready GTM brief: target segment(s) and buyer, positioning and messaging, pricing and packaging approach, channel and launch plan, key metrics and goals, and the main risks and how you'd mitigate them. Write it as you would for a launch review with the exec team.
blurb: A written GTM exercise — produce a crisp, leadership-ready launch brief with sharp positioning, a focused segment, a channel plan, and honest metrics and risks.

rubric.label: Segment & buyer
rubric.description: Identifies a focused target segment and the specific buyer/user, their pain, and buying behavior — and why to lead there — rather than 'everyone', distinguishing the economic buyer from the end user.

rubric.label: Positioning & messaging
rubric.description: Articulates sharp positioning (category, target, key benefit, differentiation vs alternatives incl. standalone AI-notetakers) and a clear value message, not a feature list.

rubric.label: Pricing & packaging
rubric.description: Proposes a defensible pricing/packaging approach (add-on vs bundled vs new tier, free trial/PLG vs sales-led) tied to value and the existing base, with rationale and tradeoffs.

rubric.label: Channel & launch plan
rubric.description: Lays out how it reaches the market — leveraging the installed base first, plus the channel mix (in-product, lifecycle, content, sales, PR/partners) and a phased launch (beta → GA) with sequencing.

rubric.label: Metrics & goals
rubric.description: Sets a north-star and funnel metrics (awareness, activation, attach/adoption rate on the base, retention, revenue) with rough targets and guardrails, and how success is judged.

rubric.label: Risks & tradeoffs
rubric.description: Names real risks (AI trust/accuracy, privacy, cannibalization, competitive standalone tools, low attach) and credible mitigations, and the tradeoffs the plan accepts.

rubric.label: Structure & writing
rubric.description: Reads like a real leadership brief: top-down, tight sections, scannable, concise, with a clear recommendation — no rambling or filler.

reference.scenario: Written GTM deliverable at the senior bar. The candidate submits a leadership-ready launch brief for an AI meeting-notes/action-item add-on to an established project-management SaaS. There's no single correct plan, but strong briefs share: a focused lead segment rather than 'everyone' (the natural wedge is the existing customer base — teams already living in the tool who run lots of meetings), a clear view of the buyer vs user (admin/team lead or economic buyer vs the individual note-taker), and sharp positioning that differentiates from both standalone AI-notetaker tools and doing-nothing — the key differentiator is that notes turn directly into tracked action items inside the PM tool the team already uses (closed loop from meeting to task), not just a transcript. Pricing/packaging is reasoned, not arbitrary: options like a paid add-on, a new higher tier, or bundling into existing plans to drive adoption, with a trial/PLG motion given the installed base, each with tradeoffs (attach revenue vs adoption vs cannibalization). The channel/launch plan leverages the installed base first (in-product prompts, lifecycle email, CSMs) before broad awareness, with a phased beta → GA sequence and a mix of in-product, content, PR, sales, and partner/integration channels. Metrics include a north-star (e.g. weekly active teams using AI notes that convert to action items) plus funnel metrics — awareness, activation, attach/adoption rate on the base, retention, and revenue — with rough targets and guardrails (e.g. AI accuracy/trust, support load, churn). Risks are honest and specific to an AI launch: accuracy/hallucination eroding trust, privacy/security of meeting content, competitive standalone notetakers, cannibalization or low attach, and over-promising AI — each with a credible mitigation. The writing is top-down, scannable, and concise, opening with a one-line recommendation. Weak briefs target 'everyone', give a feature list instead of positioning, set arbitrary pricing with no rationale, ignore the installed-base advantage, use vanity or missing metrics, hand-wave the AI trust/privacy risks, or ramble like notes rather than a leadership one-pager.
model_points: Open with a one-line recommendation/thesis (top-down): who we launch to first, the core positioning, and the primary goal for the quarter.

Target segment & buyer: lead with the installed base — existing customer teams that run many meetings and already manage work in the tool — the lowest-friction wedge. Distinguish the economic buyer (team lead/admin) from the end user (the note-taker), and their respective pains.

Positioning & messaging: sharp positioning statement — for whom, the category, the key benefit, and the differentiation. The wedge vs standalone AI-notetakers is the closed loop: meetings become tracked action items inside the PM tool the team already lives in, not just a transcript. Craft a clear value message, not a feature list.

Pricing & packaging with rationale and tradeoffs: options such as a paid add-on (maximizes attach revenue), bundling into higher tiers (drives adoption, upsell lever), or a usage/seat model — plus a trial/PLG motion given the base. Name the tradeoff each accepts (revenue vs adoption vs cannibalization).

Channel & launch plan: exploit the installed base first (in-product prompts, lifecycle email, CSM outreach) before spending on broad awareness; then the mix — content/SEO, PR/launch moment, sales for larger accounts, and integration/partner co-marketing. Phase it: closed beta with design partners → open beta → GA, with what each phase must prove.

Metrics & goals: a north-star (e.g. weekly active teams whose AI notes convert into tracked action items), plus funnel metrics — awareness/traffic, activation (first successful notes→tasks), attach/adoption rate on the existing base, retention (M1/M3), and revenue/attach — with rough targets and guardrails (AI accuracy, support load, churn, privacy incidents).

Risks & tradeoffs with mitigations, specific to an AI launch: accuracy/hallucination eroding trust (mitigate with human-in-the-loop editing, confidence signals, scoped beta), privacy/security of meeting content (clear data handling, controls, compliance messaging), competitive standalone notetakers (differentiate on the closed loop + existing workflow), cannibalization / low attach (packaging choice, positioning as additive), and over-promising AI (calibrated messaging).
State the tradeoffs the plan deliberately accepts (e.g. base-first over broad awareness this quarter; add-on revenue over fastest adoption) and the disconfirming signals that would trigger a pivot.

probes.question: Who exactly do you launch to FIRST and why them? What's your wedge into the market this quarter?
What's the one-sentence positioning — for whom, what category, what key benefit, and how is it different from a standalone AI notetaker?
Why that pricing/packaging? What does an add-on versus a bundle trade off in terms of revenue, adoption, and cannibalization?
You already have a large customer base living in the tool. How does the plan exploit that advantage before spending on cold awareness?
What's the north-star metric and a rough target, and what guardrail tells you the launch is succeeding on quality, not just signups?
What happens to trust the first time the AI mangles someone's action items or mishandles a sensitive meeting? How do you mitigate accuracy and privacy risk?
What's the sequence from beta to GA, and what does each phase have to prove before you widen it?

red_flags: Targets 'everyone' or lists many segments with no focused lead / wedge
Feature list instead of sharp positioning and a differentiated value message
Arbitrary pricing with no rationale or tradeoff analysis
Ignores the installed-base advantage; plans as if launching cold
Vanity or missing metrics; no north-star, targets, or guardrails
Hand-waves AI accuracy/trust and privacy/security risks
No phasing (beta → GA) or launch sequencing
Rambling, not top-down, reads like notes rather than a leadership brief
follow_ups: If attach on the base comes in at half your target after 30 days, what do you change first?
A competitor's free standalone AI notetaker is getting buzz. How does your positioning hold up?
How do you price this without cannibalizing your existing higher tiers?
What's the single riskiest assumption in this launch, and how would the beta test it?
Leadership will only fund half the launch budget. What survives and what's cut?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong brief opens top-down: 'Recommendation: launch AI Notes first to our existing mid-market customer base — teams that already run heavy meeting loads in our tool — positioned as ''turn every meeting into tracked action items where your work already lives,'' as a paid add-on with a free trial, targeting X% attach on the base this quarter.' Segment & buyer: 'Lead with the installed base — lowest friction, warm audience. Economic buyer is the team lead/admin who cares about follow-through and accountability; the daily user is the note-taker drowning in manual recaps.' Positioning: 'For busy teams already managing work in our platform, AI Notes is the meeting assistant that closes the loop — unlike standalone notetakers that hand you a transcript, ours turns discussion into assigned, tracked tasks in the tool your team already uses.' Pricing: 'Launch as a per-seat add-on to maximize attach revenue and signal value, with a 30-day trial to drive adoption via PLG; consider bundling into the top tier later as an upsell lever. Tradeoff: add-on protects revenue but slows adoption versus bundling — we accept that to prove willingness-to-pay first.' Channel & launch: 'Base-first — in-product prompts where meetings happen, lifecycle email, and CSM outreach to top accounts — before paid awareness; then a PR launch moment, content/SEO on meeting productivity, and integration co-marketing. Phase it: closed beta with ~15 design-partner teams to prove accuracy and the notes→tasks loop, open beta to validate activation, then GA.' Metrics: 'North-star: weekly active teams whose AI notes convert into tracked action items. Funnel: activation (first notes→tasks), attach rate on the base, M1/M3 retention, and add-on revenue — with guardrails on AI accuracy, support tickets, and privacy incidents.' Risks: 'Biggest is trust — a mangled action item or a mishandled sensitive meeting erodes confidence, so we ship human-in-the-loop editing, confidence cues, clear data-handling controls, and a scoped beta; competitive standalone tools we counter on the closed-loop differentiation; cannibalization we manage via packaging.' It's tight, top-down, scannable, and makes a real recommendation with honest tradeoffs — a brief an exec team could act on in two minutes.

interviewer_notes: This is a WRITTEN deliverable — evaluate the artifact, not a live dialogue. The senior bar is a genuine GTM strategy: a focused lead segment and wedge (the installed base), sharp differentiated positioning (the closed loop vs standalone notetakers), reasoned pricing with tradeoffs, an installed-base-first channel plan with beta→GA phasing, real metrics with targets and guardrails, and honest AI-specific risks (accuracy/trust, privacy) with mitigations. Reward top-down structure that opens with a recommendation and is scannable. The most common senior-level misses are targeting 'everyone', giving a feature list instead of positioning, ignoring the installed-base advantage, and hand-waving AI trust/privacy. If used interactively, deliver the probes as written feedback prompting a revision. Judge writing quality and concision as part of the score — a leadership brief must be tight and decision-oriented.
